modalities.whatItIs: Eyes Open Shaking is a new, untested concept that pushes tremor-based practice as far as possible from inner imagery, memory and guidance. After tiring the legs until they begin to tremble, you let the tremor run with your eyes open, keeping your attention on what you can actually see, hear and touch right now. It is fully self-led, present-focused and allowing: nothing is pictured, remembered or worked on.
modalities.coreIdea: Staying oriented to the real surroundings while the body shakes is meant to keep the practice grounded in the present and stop it drifting into old memories or imagined scenes.
modalities.whatYouDo: You do 15 minutes of leg-tiring exercises, such as wall sits, slow lunges and calf raises, until your thighs feel tired and a little shaky. Then you lie on a mat with knees bent and eyes open, letting the legs tremble for up to 15 minutes while you silently name things you see on the ceiling, sounds in the room and the feel of the floor under your back. You stop at any time by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who drift into memories or worry when they close their eyes, and who want a simple, physical way to unwind that keeps them anchored in the here and now.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: the tiring exercises are moderately hard, so check with a doctor first if you have heart problems, epilepsy, recent injuries or surgery, or are pregnant, and stop if you feel pain, dizziness or panic. People with trauma, dissociation or a serious mental health condition should learn tremor practices only with a clinically trained provider.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Eyes Open Shaking. Tire your legs with a few wall sits, lie down, and let them tremble while you keep your eyes open and name what you see and hear. Body busy, mind in the room. For people who drift into worry the moment they close their eyes.

modalities.name: Hands on the Tremor
modalities.tagline: Resting your own hands on your body to feel the tremor directly.
modalities.whatItIs: Hands on the Tremor is a proposed self-led variation of tremor-based practice that keeps attention entirely on direct physical contact, the opposite of inner work with imagined figures or parts. While the legs tremble, you place your own hands, in a set order, on the thighs, belly and chest to feel the movement under your palms. It is calm, structured and done alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Feeling the tremor through your own hands gives the mind one simple, present thing to follow, which is meant to make the practice steadier and more settling than watching it from inside.
modalities.whatYouDo: After ten to fifteen minutes of leg-tiring exercises, you lie on your back with knees bent and let the tremor start. You then rest your hands for three minutes each on your thighs, your lower belly and the center of your chest, simply feeling the tremor or stillness under your palms, and finish with both hands on the belly for a few slow breaths. A session takes about 30 minutes, and you can stop at any point by straightening your legs.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find body practices too vague or floaty, who like having something concrete to do, and who find steady touch comforting.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: check with a doctor first if you have heart problems, epilepsy or injuries, or are pregnant, since the tiring exercises are moderately hard. Strong emotions can surface during tremor practice, so people with trauma, dissociation or a serious mental health condition should learn it with a clinically trained provider.
modalities.tweet: For anyone who finds body practices too vague, an idea: tire your legs, lie down, let them tremble, and rest your own hands on your thighs, belly and chest to feel it under your palms. Calm, simple, something concrete to hold on to. Untested, so go gently.

modalities.name: Nothing Has to Happen
modalities.tagline: A tremor practice with no goal, no counting and no right result.
modalities.whatItIs: Nothing Has to Happen is a new, untested concept that takes tremor-based practice as far as possible from goal-setting, tracking and deliberate change. You tire the legs and lie down, but you do not try to make a tremor start, last or feel a certain way. Whatever the body does, whether shaking, stillness, yawning, sighing or sleepiness, is equally welcome.
modalities.coreIdea: Trying hard to get a 'good' session can turn a body practice into another task to fail at, so dropping every target is meant to leave the body free to do whatever it does.
modalities.whatYouDo: You do whichever leg-tiring exercises feel right that day for ten minutes or so, then lie down on a mat or rug, knees bent, for as long as you like. If a tremor comes, you let it; if it does not, you simply rest and notice the floor, your breath and the sounds around you. You keep no log and give no ratings, and you stop whenever you have had enough.
modalities.whoItsFor: Perfectionists and people who turn every practice into a performance, and anyone who wants a body practice that asks nothing of them.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: the tiring exercises can strain the heart and joints, so check with a doctor first if you have heart problems, injuries or epilepsy, or are pregnant. Feelings or memories can surface while lying still, so stop if you feel overwhelmed, and people with trauma or dissociation should learn tremor practices with a clinically trained provider.
modalities.tweet: Untested concept: Nothing Has to Happen. Tire your legs a little, lie down, and let the body do whatever it does: tremble, rest, yawn, nothing at all. No goal, no counting, no right result. For people who turn even relaxing into a test 🌿

modalities.name: Tremor in Color
modalities.tagline: Drawing where the tremor went, session after session, without words.
modalities.whatItIs: Tremor in Color is a proposed solitary variation of tremor-based practice that moves even further from talk, values and mental exercises than the original. After each session you color a simple outline of a body to show where you felt tremor, tension or warmth, without writing a single word. Over weeks, the maps build a private, picture-only record of how your body responds.
modalities.coreIdea: Keeping the record in pictures rather than words is meant to keep attention on the body itself, and the growing pile of maps may show patterns that a diary of thoughts would miss.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you do a structured 30-minute session: 15 minutes of set leg-tiring exercises, up to 15 minutes lying down letting the tremor run, then two minutes with colored pencils and a printed body outline. You use one color for tremor, one for tension and one for ease, and date the page. Every month you lay the maps side by side and simply look, without analyzing.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are tired of talking about their feelings, who think visually, or who want to notice how their body changes over time without keeping a diary.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: the maps are a personal record, not a medical test, so see a doctor about any new pain, numbness or unusual shaking. Check with a doctor before starting if you have heart problems, epilepsy or injuries, or are pregnant, and learn tremor practices with a clinically trained provider if you have trauma or dissociation.
modalities.tweet: Concept: after each body-shaking session, you color a simple body outline to show where you felt tremor, tension or ease. No words at all. Over weeks the maps become a picture diary of your body. For people who are tired of talking about feelings.

modalities.name: Plain Muscle Shake
modalities.tagline: Tired muscles shake, and that is all it needs to mean.
modalities.whatItIs: Plain Muscle Shake is a new, untested concept that strips tremor-based practice of every story about trauma, energy or hidden meaning, the opposite of approaches that search for the emotional truth behind a symptom. It explains the shaking simply as what tired muscles do, and invites you to enjoy it as a calming, physical experience. It is self-led, quiet and present-focused.
modalities.coreIdea: You do not need to believe that shaking releases anything for it to feel pleasant and settling, so the practice keeps the experience and drops the theory.
modalities.whatYouDo: You tire your legs with a few minutes of wall sits and slow squats until they feel shaky, then lie down with knees bent for ten to fifteen minutes and let them tremble. If your mind starts looking for meaning ('what is coming out of me?'), you remind yourself 'these are tired muscles' and go back to the plain feel of the movement. Afterwards you rest for a few minutes before getting up.
modalities.whoItsFor: Skeptics who like the feel of shaking practices but not the claims around them, and anyone who wants a simple, calming wind-down with nothing to interpret.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: the exercises are moderately hard, so check with a doctor first if you have heart problems, epilepsy or injuries, or are pregnant, and stop if you feel pain or dizziness. Even without any story, strong feelings can surface, so pause if you feel overwhelmed, and seek a clinically trained provider if you have trauma or dissociation.
modalities.tweet: A skeptic-friendly idea: Plain Muscle Shake. Tire your legs, lie down, let them tremble. No talk of releasing trauma or energy, just tired muscles doing what tired muscles do. For people who like how shaking feels but not the claims around it.

modalities.name: Upright Tremble
modalities.tagline: Letting the tremor run while standing, eyes open, holding a wall.
modalities.whatItIs: Upright Tremble is a proposed active variation of tremor-based practice that moves away from slow, inward, still attention and toward standing, outward, physical engagement. Instead of lying down after the tiring exercises, you stay on your feet, holding a wall or sturdy chair, and let the tremor run through bent knees and hips. It is structured, a little more energetic than lying practice, and learned from a trained provider.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting the body shake while upright and alert is meant to link the tremor with everyday standing life, so the practice feels active and outward rather than inward and sleepy.
modalities.whatYouDo: After 15 minutes of set leg-tiring exercises, you stand with feet hip-width apart, one hand on a wall, and soften your knees until a tremor starts in the thighs. For up to ten minutes you let it run, adjusting the bend of your knees to make it gentler or stronger, with eyes open and attention on the room. You finish by standing still for a minute, then walking slowly around the room.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get sleepy or lost in thought lying down, who prefer to stay on their feet, and who like a more energetic, outward-facing practice.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: shaking while standing carries a risk of losing balance, so always hold a wall or sturdy chair, keep the area clear, and sit down if you feel dizzy. Check with a doctor first if you have heart, balance or joint problems or epilepsy, or are pregnant, and learn it with a clinically trained provider if you have trauma or dissociation.
modalities.tweet: Imagine a shaking practice you do on your feet: tire your legs, hold a wall, soften your knees and let the tremor run while you look around the room. A new, more upright take for people who get sleepy or lost in thought lying down. Hold on to something!

modalities.name: The Eight-Week Ladder
modalities.tagline: A self-coached, step-by-step plan for building a home shaking practice.
modalities.whatItIs: The Eight-Week Ladder is a new, untested concept that turns tremor-based practice into a structured, self-run progression, the opposite of open, presence-based coaching. A printed plan sets out eight weekly rungs, each adding a little more tremor time or a new position, with clear rules for when to stay on a rung. You follow it alone and judge your own progress against simple checks.
modalities.coreIdea: Building up gradually and predictably is meant to make a home shaking practice safer and easier to keep, because you always know the next small step and when to hold back.
modalities.whatYouDo: In week one you do the tiring exercises and allow just three minutes of tremor, three times a week; each week adds two or three minutes or a new variation, such as feet flat or knees wider. You move up a rung only if the last week felt comfortable, and drop back one rung after any session that left you shaky, tearful or wired. A short checklist after each session records time, comfort and anything to watch.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like plans and gradual progress, who want to practice at home without a teacher every week, and who appreciate clear rules for going slowly.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea, and the usual advice is to learn tremor practices first with a certified provider, especially with any history of trauma, dissociation or serious mental health conditions. Check with a doctor before starting if you have heart problems, epilepsy or injuries, or are pregnant.
modalities.tweet: A proposal for building a home shaking practice: The Eight-Week Ladder. Start with three minutes of tremor, add a little each week, and drop back a rung whenever a session leaves you wired or teary. For people who like plans and going slowly.

modalities.name: Dial the Tremor
modalities.tagline: Training yourself to turn a tremor up, down and off on cue.
modalities.whatItIs: Dial the Tremor is a proposed precise, provider-taught variation of tremor-based practice that makes control the whole point, the far opposite of letting go of all intention. You learn to raise, lower and stop the tremor at set moments by changing leg position, like turning a dimmer switch. Sessions follow an exact script with counts and timings.
modalities.coreIdea: Being able to turn a body reaction up and down on purpose is meant to build a felt sense of being in charge of it, which may make the practice feel safer and more predictable.
modalities.whatYouDo: After the standard tiring exercises, you lie down and follow a timed script, often with a provider counting: one minute of gentle tremor with knees close together, one minute stronger with knees apart, thirty seconds stopped with legs straight, then repeat four times. You rate how well you could match each level on a simple 0 to 3 scale. Once you can follow the script reliably, you practice it at home twice a week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel uneasy letting the body move on its own, who want to know they can stop at any moment, and who like precise, measurable practice.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: the exercises are moderately hard, so check with a doctor first if you have heart problems, epilepsy or injuries, or are pregnant. Learn it with a clinically trained provider if you have trauma or dissociation, and stop if you feel pain, panic or spaced out.
modalities.tweet: Speculative twist on body shaking: Dial the Tremor. You learn to turn the tremor up, down and off on cue by moving your knees, following a timed script. Less 'let go', more 'I'm in charge'. For people uneasy about letting the body move on its own.

modalities.name: The Honest Ache
modalities.tagline: Meeting the plain ache of tired muscles openly, without chasing pleasant states.
modalities.whatItIs: The Honest Ache is a new, untested concept that turns tremor-based practice away from cultivating warm, blissful or absorbed states and toward plain, honest contact with ordinary sensation. During the tiring phase and the tremor that follows, you give open attention to the ache, burn and heaviness of tired muscles, neither pushing it away nor trying to turn it into something pleasant. It is allowing and sensory, and is learned from a provider before practicing alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Practicing openness to mild, safe discomfort in the body, rather than chasing good feelings, is meant to build a simple, steady way of being with sensation as it is.
modalities.whatYouDo: You hold a wall sit for one to two minutes and, instead of distracting yourself, notice exactly where the ache is, how it pulses and how it changes. Then you lie down and let the tremor run for up to 15 minutes, noticing whatever the tired muscles feel, pleasant or not. You come out of the wall sit at once if the sensation turns sharp or painful.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tend to run from discomfort, who have found blissful meditations frustrating or out of reach, and who like a plain, physical way to practice openness.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: aim only for mild muscle fatigue, never sharp or joint pain, and check with a doctor first if you have heart problems, injuries or epilepsy, or are pregnant. Strong feelings can surface, so stop if you feel overwhelmed, and learn it with a clinically trained provider if you have trauma or dissociation.
modalities.tweet: Hypothetical practice: The Honest Ache. During a wall sit and the leg tremor after it, you meet the plain ache of tired muscles with open attention, not chasing bliss or escaping it. Mild fatigue only, never sharp pain. For people who run from discomfort.

modalities.name: Sigh and Tremble
modalities.tagline: Letting sighs, hums and sounds out as the body shakes.
modalities.whatItIs: Sigh and Tremble is a proposed variation of tremor-based practice that moves away from silent, still observation and lets the voice join in. While the legs tremble, you allow long sighs, hums or soft sounds to come out with the breath instead of keeping quiet. It is a little more active and expressive than plain tremor practice, and is learned from a provider.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting breath and voice move with the body, rather than holding them still while watching, is meant to make the practice feel fuller and less controlled.
modalities.whatYouDo: After 15 minutes of tiring exercises, you lie down with knees bent and let the tremor start, then breathe out through the mouth in long sighs, adding a soft hum or 'ahh' whenever it feels natural. You do not perform or force sounds; you simply stop holding them back, for up to 15 minutes. You end with a minute of quiet breathing before rolling onto your side to get up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who hold their breath or clench their jaw when stressed, who find silent practice tense, and who have a private space where they can make some noise.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: forced or very deep breathing can cause dizziness or tingling, so keep sighs relaxed and stop if you feel lightheaded. Check with a doctor first if you have heart or breathing problems or epilepsy, or are pregnant, and learn it with a clinically trained provider if you have trauma or dissociation.
modalities.tweet: Do you hold your breath when stressed? An idea: Sigh and Tremble. Tire your legs, lie down, let them shake, and let long sighs and soft hums out with the breath. A louder, looser body practice for people who clench their jaw and keep everything in.

modalities.name: The Resting Quiver
modalities.tagline: A near-effortless tremor practice for a bed, sofa or armchair.
modalities.whatItIs: The Resting Quiver is a new, untested concept that strips tremor-based practice of almost all effort, the far opposite of hard, fast interval training. There are no wall sits or lunges: a few minutes of gentle, held positions in bed or a chair are used to invite a soft quiver, and the aim is to stay as calm and unhurried as possible. It is loosely structured, very allowing, and learned from a provider who adapts it to your body.
modalities.coreIdea: Some people cannot or should not do vigorous tiring exercises, so the practice looks for the smallest, softest way into a settling tremor, with calm as the priority throughout.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lying in bed or sitting well supported in an armchair, you gently press your knees together for a minute, let go, then rest your feet flat and let the knees drift slightly apart, noticing any small quiver in the thighs. If one comes, you let it run softly for a few minutes; if not, you simply rest and breathe slowly. A session takes 10 to 20 minutes and can end in sleep or rest.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with low energy, limited mobility, long-term illness or older bodies who find standard exercises too demanding, and anyone who wants the calmest possible version.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea and should be adapted with a provider and, where relevant, your doctor or physiotherapist, especially with a neurological condition, recent surgery or a condition that already causes tremor. New or unexplained shaking should always be checked by a doctor rather than practiced with.
modalities.tweet: Untested and gentle: The Resting Quiver, a shaking practice with almost no effort. No wall sits, just gentle held positions in bed or an armchair, a soft quiver if it comes, and lots of rest. For people with low energy, limited mobility or a tired body.

modalities.name: The Lights-Out Shake
modalities.tagline: A quiet, solitary shaking routine for the last twenty minutes before sleep.
modalities.whatItIs: The Lights-Out Shake is a proposed solitary, night-time version of tremor-based practice, the opposite of loud, competitive, sociable sport. It uses only gentle tiring movements and a dim, quiet room, and ends in bed with the lights off. A provider helps you set up the routine, and then it is the same every night.
modalities.coreIdea: Doing the same gentle, calming body routine alone at the end of every day is meant to signal to the body that the day is over and make the shift toward sleep feel easier.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twenty minutes before bed, with lights low and phone in another room, you do five minutes of slow calf raises and gentle knee bends, then lie on your bed with knees bent and let any light tremor run for up to ten minutes. When it fades, you stretch out your legs, notice the weight of the blanket and breathe slowly until you are ready to sleep. The order and timing stay the same every night.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who lie awake replaying the day, who come home wired from busy, social or noisy days, and who like a simple, private bedtime ritual.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea and not a sleep treatment: ongoing insomnia, loud snoring or daytime sleepiness should be checked by a doctor. Strong emotions can surface when lying still, so if bedtime tremor stirs things up, move it earlier in the evening, and people with trauma or dissociation should learn it with a clinically trained provider.
modalities.tweet: Imagined bedtime ritual: The Lights-Out Shake. Lights low, phone away, five minutes of gentle calf raises, then lie down and let any soft tremor run until it fades. Same routine every night. For people who lie awake replaying the day 🌙

modalities.name: Counted Exhale Shake
modalities.tagline: Slow, counted out-breaths paced through a gentle body tremor.
modalities.whatItIs: Counted Exhale Shake is a new, untested concept that pairs tremor-based practice with slow, counted breathing, turning away from long, continuous effort toward short, calm, structured sessions. During the tremor phase you breathe out for longer than you breathe in, following a set count taught by a provider. The tiring phase is light, so the whole session stays gentle.
modalities.coreIdea: Slow breathing with long out-breaths is widely used to settle the body, and pacing the breath through a gentle tremor is meant to give the practice a steady, calming rhythm.
modalities.whatYouDo: A provider first teaches you the routine in one or two sessions, and you then practice at home. After five minutes of light tiring exercises, you lie down, let a gentle tremor start, and breathe in for a count of four and out for a count of six or seven, for ten minutes. You finish with two minutes of normal breathing, and check in with the provider once a month.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel keyed up and want a very calm, structured routine, and who find it easier to settle when they have a breathing count to follow.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: stop if counting the breath makes you anxious, dizzy or short of breath, and people with asthma, lung or heart conditions should check with a doctor first. Learn tremor practices with a clinically trained provider if you have trauma or dissociation.
modalities.tweet: A new pairing: Counted Exhale Shake. A light leg tremor plus slow counted breathing, in for four and out for six or seven, for ten calm minutes. For keyed-up people who settle more easily with a count to follow than with 'just relax'.

modalities.name: Stretch-Born Tremor
modalities.tagline: Inviting a soft tremor through long, gentle stretches instead of tiring muscles.
modalities.whatItIs: Stretch-Born Tremor is a proposed variation of tremor-based practice that drops the load and effort of tiring exercises, the opposite of strength training. Instead, a soft tremor is invited through long, gentle stretches held at an easy edge, and whatever happens is allowed. It is loosely structured, very accepting and learned from a provider.
modalities.coreIdea: A long, easy stretch can sometimes set off a small natural tremor, and following that softly, without straining or pushing, is meant to make shaking practice gentler on joints and the heart.
modalities.whatYouDo: You lie on your back and, for two to three minutes each, hold easy stretches such as one knee to the chest, a butterfly position with the soles of the feet together, or legs resting up a wall. If a small tremor appears, you let it run and stay with the stretch; if not, you breathe and move on to the next. A session takes 20 to 30 minutes and ends with a few minutes lying flat.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find wall sits and squats too hard on their knees or heart, who prefer slow, soft movement, and who want a gentle way into shaking practice.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: stretch only to a comfortable edge, never into pain, and take extra care with hypermobile joints, recent injuries, hip or back problems or pregnancy, checking with a doctor or physiotherapist first. Learn tremor practices with a clinically trained provider if you have trauma or dissociation.
modalities.tweet: Here's a softer idea: Stretch-Born Tremor. Instead of wall sits, you hold long, easy stretches (knee to chest, legs up a wall) and let any small tremor that appears just run. No load, no strain. For people whose knees or heart don't love squats.

modalities.name: The Travel Shake
modalities.tagline: A short, self-run shaking routine that needs no mat, teacher or company.
modalities.whatItIs: The Travel Shake is a new, untested concept that makes tremor-based practice fully portable and self-reliant, the opposite of sessions built around a trained animal and its handler. It is a fixed, 15-minute routine you can do alone in a hotel room, an office or a quiet corner, with no mat or equipment. Once learned, it needs nobody else.
modalities.coreIdea: Keeping one short, memorized routine that fits any floor or chair is meant to let you settle your body wherever you are, without relying on a place, a person or a pet.
modalities.whatYouDo: You stand and do three set moves for two minutes each, such as calf raises, a wall sit against a door and slow lunges, then sit on the edge of a chair or lie on a towel with knees bent and let a tremor run for up to five minutes. You end by standing, shaking out your hands, and taking three slow breaths. The routine never changes, so you can do it without thinking.
modalities.whoItsFor: Travelers, shift workers and busy people who want a quick, private way to unwind in any space, without needing a class or another person.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: learn the basics with a certified provider first, and check with a doctor if you have heart problems, epilepsy or injuries, or are pregnant. Practicing alone means nobody is there if strong feelings surface, so keep sessions short and stop if you feel overwhelmed or spaced out.
modalities.tweet: An invented routine for travelers and shift workers: The Travel Shake. Three moves, two minutes each, then let your legs tremble for up to five minutes on a towel or chair. No mat, no class, no company needed. A portable way to unwind ✈️

modalities.name: Everyday Fatigue Shake
modalities.tagline: Using the tiredness of ordinary days instead of a set exercise form.
modalities.whatItIs: Everyday Fatigue Shake is a proposed loose, unscripted variation of tremor-based practice, moving away from fixed, flowing movement forms. Instead of doing set tiring exercises, you use the natural tiredness your legs already have after a long walk, a day on your feet, climbing stairs or gardening. When it is there, you lie down and let a tremor come.
modalities.coreIdea: Ordinary life already tires the body, so borrowing that tiredness, rather than adding a workout, is meant to fold the practice into the day and keep it simple and flexible.
modalities.whatYouDo: On days when your legs feel heavy, for example after a hike or a long shift, you find ten to twenty minutes to lie on the floor with knees bent and feet flat. You wait for a tremor to start in the thighs and let it run, changing position by feel rather than by a script. If no tremor comes, you simply rest, and you never add extra effort to force one.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who already move a lot in daily life, who dislike fixed routines, and who want a flexible practice that fits around real days.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: do not use it after an injury, a fall or unusual pain, which need a doctor instead, and check with a doctor first if you have heart problems or epilepsy, or are pregnant. Strong feelings can surface, so stop if you feel overwhelmed, and learn tremor practices with a clinically trained provider if you have trauma or dissociation.
modalities.tweet: Novel idea: Everyday Fatigue Shake. Skip the set exercises and use the tiredness life already gave you (a long walk, a day on your feet), then lie down and let your legs tremble. For people who move a lot and hate fixed routines.

modalities.name: Before the World Wakes
modalities.tagline: A fixed, solitary dawn routine before any people, news or screens.
modalities.whatItIs: Before the World Wakes is a new, untested concept that turns tremor-based practice into a strictly solitary morning ritual, the opposite of seeking out social contact. Each day starts with the same set sequence, done alone before you speak to anyone, check messages or read the news. A provider designs the sequence with you and checks in every few weeks.
modalities.coreIdea: Meeting your own body first, in silence and solitude, before the day's demands arrive is meant to give a calm, steady starting point that belongs to you alone.
modalities.whatYouDo: Right after waking, with your phone still off, you do a fixed 25-minute sequence: five minutes of gentle stretches, ten minutes of set leg-tiring exercises, and up to ten minutes lying down letting the tremor run. You finish by sitting quietly for one minute before switching anything on. The provider reviews the routine with you monthly and adjusts it if mornings feel rushed or unsettled.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose days fill up with other people's needs from the moment they wake, such as parents, carers and people in demanding jobs, and who want a private start to the day.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: muscles and joints are stiffer in the morning, so warm up gently, and check with a doctor first if you have heart problems, epilepsy or injuries, or are pregnant. If strong feelings come up and color the whole day, move practice to a later time, and learn it with a clinically trained provider if you have trauma or dissociation.
modalities.tweet: Imagine meeting your own body each morning before your inbox. A new concept: Before the World Wakes. Phone off, stretches, a few leg exercises, then a quiet tremor on the floor, alone. For parents, carers and anyone whose day starts at full speed.

modalities.name: Personal Tremor Trial
modalities.tagline: A careful indoor experiment to see what tremor practice does for you.
modalities.whatItIs: Personal Tremor Trial is a proposed, highly structured way to try tremor-based practice as a personal experiment, the opposite of an open, wandering walk outdoors. With a provider's help, you follow an exact indoor protocol for six weeks and rate a few simple things before and after each session. The point is to find out honestly what, if anything, changes for you.
modalities.coreIdea: Since the research on tremor practices is thin, running a careful, written trial on yourself is meant to replace hopes and claims with your own honest observations.
modalities.whatYouDo: A provider helps you set up the protocol: the same indoor space, time and sequence each session, with timed tiring exercises and a fixed tremor period. Before and after each session you rate muscle tension, mood and calm from 0 to 10, and on alternate weeks you replace the tremor with plain rest for comparison. At the end, you and the provider look at the numbers together and decide whether to continue.
modalities.whoItsFor: Curious skeptics, people who like data, and anyone who wants to know whether shaking practice actually suits them before committing to it.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea, and a personal trial cannot prove anything about tremor practice in general, so keep the results in perspective. Check with a doctor first if you have heart problems, epilepsy or injuries, or are pregnant, and learn it with a clinically trained provider if you have trauma or dissociation.
modalities.tweet: Experimental mindset, literally: the Personal Tremor Trial. Six weeks of the same indoor shaking routine, rating tension and calm before and after, with plain-rest weeks for comparison. Then you look at your own numbers. For curious skeptics 📊

modalities.name: Shake, Then Debrief
modalities.tagline: A tremor session followed by a short, guided look at what surfaced.
modalities.whatItIs: Shake, Then Debrief is a new, untested concept that adds a short, provider-led reflection to every tremor session, moving away from pure, self-guided sensory attention. After a structured tiring phase and tremor, a trained provider spends ten minutes helping you notice which feelings, images or memories came up. Nothing is dug into; the aim is simply to notice and put a few words to it.
modalities.coreIdea: Strong feelings sometimes surface during tremor practice, and a brief, guided debrief is meant to help you make sense of them gently instead of being left alone with them.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 45-minute one-to-one session, you do 15 minutes of set tiring exercises and up to 15 minutes of tremor, then sit up with a drink of water. The provider asks a few simple questions, such as 'what did you notice?' and 'is there anything you want to leave here?', and helps you settle before you leave. Sessions are weekly for six weeks, with home practice allowed once the provider agrees.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find that shaking practice stirs feelings or memories, and who want a little support to process them without moving into full talking therapy.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: the debrief is not therapy, and if memories of trauma come up, the provider should pause the practice and help you find a clinician trained in trauma care. Check with a doctor first if you have heart problems, epilepsy or injuries, or are pregnant.
modalities.tweet: Proposed format: Shake, Then Debrief. A weekly session of leg exercises and tremor, then ten minutes with a trained provider gently noticing what came up. Not therapy, just not being left alone with it. For people whose body practice stirs things up.

modalities.name: No Soundtrack Shaking
modalities.tagline: A tremor practice in full silence: no music, no voice, no app.
modalities.whatItIs: No Soundtrack Shaking is a proposed solitary, silent variation of tremor-based practice, the opposite of using music to shape mood. There is no playlist, no guiding voice and no app: you follow a memorized, fixed sequence in a quiet room, and the only sounds are your breath, the floor and the room. It is calm, structured and done alone after learning it from a provider.
modalities.coreIdea: Without music or guidance telling the body how to feel, attention rests on the plain sounds and sensations of the practice itself, which is meant to make it quieter and more your own.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a quiet room with devices off, you do your memorized sequence of leg-tiring exercises for about 15 minutes, counting silently. Then you lie down and let the tremor run for up to 15 minutes, listening only to your breath, the creak of the floor and any sounds from outside. You end with a minute of stillness before getting up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who usually fill every moment with music or podcasts, who are curious what their body is like in silence, and who like simple, self-run routines.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: silence can make it easier for difficult thoughts or feelings to surface, so stop if you feel overwhelmed or spaced out. Check with a doctor first if you have heart problems, epilepsy or injuries, or are pregnant, and learn it with a clinically trained provider if you have trauma or dissociation.
modalities.tweet: Prototype for the always-on-headphones crowd: No Soundtrack Shaking. A short leg routine and a quiet tremor on the floor, with no music, no guiding voice, no app. Just your breath and the room. What's your body like in silence?
